question: to the Commission Nicolás González Casares (S&D), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D) Subject:

The mobile game Age of Origins allegedly uses manipulative monetisation systems, including dark patterns, misleading advertising and simulated gambling mechanics, to encourage spending by users. Concerns have been raised about inadequate moderation of hate speech and violent threats within the game’s social environment, and inconsistent Pan-European Game Information (PEGI) ratings across platforms. The game also promoted speculative crypto-assets whose collapse caused financial losses to users. Questions arise as to whether Apple and Alphabet (Google Play) fulfilled their responsibilities under EU consumer protection law, namely the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). In this context: 1.

Does the Commission consider that very large online platforms under the DSA and app store operators designated as ‘gatekeepers’ under the DMA bear greater responsibility when profiting from harmful or unlawful monetisation and crypto-asset systems targeting minors?

If so, will the Commission consider launching an investigation or coordinated enforcement action into the systemic risks that mobile gaming ecosystems may pose to consumers’ mental health, financial security and fundamental rights?

How will the Commission strengthen EU-wide protection for minors against loot boxes (randomised in-game purchases with unknown rewards), simulated gambling and manipulative monetisation mechanisms in online games through the upcoming Digital Fairness Act and the revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) In recognition of their extensive reach and influence, the Digital Services Act (DSA)1 places additional obligations on designated very large online platforms like Google Play and Apple App Store. Their provider must at least annually diligently identify, assess and mitigate systemic risks on their services, including negative impacts on the wellbeing of minors. The DSA guidelines on the protection of minors2 contain measures to shield minors from certain commercial practices on online platforms that could negatively impact their privacy, safety and security. For example, minors should not be exposed to methods that make financial transactions untransparent or potentially misleading like virtual currencies. The Commission is diligently enforcing the DSA. In September 2025, the Commission asked the Apple App Store and Google Play to provide detailed information on how they assess the presence of fraudulent content and the measures they take to reduce the risks of financial scams, including fraudulent applications imitating legitimate banking, investment or trading apps. In October 2025, the Commission requested information from the Apple App Store and Google Play regarding their measures to ensure that minors are not exposed to harmful apps, like gambling apps, and the effectiveness of their age rating systems. At the national level, for example, the German Bundesnetzagentur is investigating the gaming platform Steam due to possible breaches of the DSA in connection with the Plantation Simulator video game. The ongoing impact assessment for the Digital Fairness Act3 examines if further action is needed to address specific practices like gambling-simulating features (loot boxes) or pay-towin and pay-to-progress features that are widely used in video games. The revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation4 will aim to ensure stronger, faster and more deterrent enforcement of EU consumer law, thus also contributing to an enhanced protection of young consumers, including in the digital world.
